prompt: What is a technical reputation, by the lesson?
hint: When you are not in the room.

choices.text: The number of talks given and articles published in a year
choices.why: Count is not what people expect of you.

choices.text: Your title and seniority
choices.why: Titles are given; reputation is earned from evidence.

choices.text: What people expect of you, built from work they saw
choices.why: Right: a record, not a brand.

choices.text: A personal brand, managed with posts and profiles
choices.why: The picture the lesson starts by rejecting.

prompt: Put the rings of a reputation in the order the lesson builds them.
What is a brag document, in Julia Evans's sense?

choices.text: A complaint about credit taken by others
choices.why: No.

choices.text: A CV written in the first person, with every achievement bolded
choices.why: Not a CV.

choices.text: A public post listing your achievements
choices.why: It is private, a source for reviews and memory.

choices.text: A running list of what you did and what came of it
choices.why: Right: updated every few weeks.

prompt: What does the lesson say every document in this course also was?

choices.text: Wasted time that could have gone into code
choices.why: The course argues the opposite.

choices.text: Evidence for Lívia's next promotion case, written on purpose with that in mind
choices.why: Written for readers, not for a promotion.

choices.text: A piece of reputation
choices.why: Right: the visible residue of doing the work well and writing it down.

choices.text: A template for other teams
choices.why: Some became templates; that is not the point made.

prompt: Which conditions did Marola set on Lívia's article? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: No security detail
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: No client names
choices.why: Yes: Boa Praça does not appear.

choices.text: No revenue or order numbers
choices.why: Yes: competitors read them.

choices.text: No mention of failures
choices.why: The failures are what made it worth reading.

prompt: Which rows of a useful article does the lesson say most company posts are weakest at?

choices.text: What worked
choices.why: Posts are usually strongest here.

choices.text: The problem and what happened
choices.why: Most posts manage these.

choices.text: The title and the headings, which are written last
choices.why: Lesson 1 matters there, and it is not the weak point named.

choices.text: What we would change, and what is still unknown
choices.why: Right: without them it reads as an advertisement.

prompt: When did Lívia ask permission to write about the incident?

choices.text: After publishing, if anybody objected
choices.why: Too late to change what was said.

choices.text: Never; engineering blogs need no approval
choices.why: Most of what an engineer knows belongs to the employer.

choices.text: Before drafting, with a short outline
choices.why: Right: the conditions then shaped the article.

choices.text: After the full draft was finished and edited
choices.why: Then the conditions would have meant rewriting it.

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend a local meetup as a first venue?

choices.text: Friendly audience, short slot, organisers looking for speakers
choices.why: Right: and a talk given once is easier to give again.

choices.text: Conferences do not accept first-time speakers
choices.why: Not claimed.

choices.text: Nobody records meetup talks, so mistakes are forgotten
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: Meetups pay their speakers
choices.why: Not mentioned.

prompt: Which part of a talk does the lesson suggest knowing by heart?

choices.text: All of it, word for word
choices.why: Not suggested; it sounds recited.

choices.text: The first two minutes
choices.why: Right: nerves are worst at the start.

choices.text: The closing slide
choices.why: Not the part named.

choices.text: The answers to every possible question from the room
choices.why: Lesson 5 says prepare the three hardest.

pairs.left: a bug report with a minimal reproducer
a test for a behaviour you depend on

prompt: Before contributing code that came from work to an open-source project, what should an engineer do?

choices.text: Contribute it under a personal account
choices.why: That hides the question rather than answering it.

choices.text: Read the company's policy, or ask
choices.why: Right: Marola asks for a lead's check before code.

choices.text: Wait until leaving the company to contribute anything at all
choices.why: Docs and bug reports are free at Marola.

choices.text: Nothing, if the project's licence is permissive
choices.why: The question is the employer's policy, not the project's licence.

prompt: Which line follows the lesson's rule about credit?

choices.text: "I built the connection quotas."
choices.why: Bruna's team built them.

choices.text: "The quotas were built." (no subject)
choices.why: Passive hiding the actor, lesson 1.

choices.text: "Bruna's team built the quotas; Lucas wrote the alert."
choices.why: Right: names wherever the people are happy to be named.

choices.text: "Marola's engineering team built them."
choices.why: Accurate, and it hides who did it.

prompt: By the lesson, what separates building a reputation from selling yourself?

choices.text: Whether the talk is internal or public
choices.why: Either can be either.

choices.text: Whether they learn about the subject or about you
choices.why: Right: teaching is visibility that lasts.

choices.text: Whether you are paid for the talk
choices.why: Not the line drawn.

choices.text: How many people come to listen to it
choices.why: Audience size is not the test.

prompt: Why is honesty about failure the most credible signal a speaker can send?

choices.text: It costs something nobody only selling would pay
choices.why: Right: that is why it is believed.

choices.text: Conferences require a failures section
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: It makes the speaker seem humble
choices.why: Seeming is not the mechanism.

choices.text: Audiences enjoy stories of failure more
choices.why: Enjoyment is not credibility.

prompt: Lívia's talk praises a tool whose maker sponsors the meetup. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Remove the praise
choices.why: The praise may be deserved; the interest must be declared.

choices.text: Decline to give the talk at a sponsored event
choices.why: Not required.

choices.text: Declare it at the start
choices.why: Right: one sentence is enough.

choices.text: Nothing, since sponsors do not affect content
choices.why: An undeclared interest turns the talk into an advertisement in retrospect.

prompt: The idea the course ends on: the work is not finished until the people who need it ___ it.
A colleague asks Lívia to speak on a panel about a database she has never used. Following lessons 8 and 16, what is her best answer?
hint: A no with an alternative, and sponsorship.

choices.text: Accept, and read up beforehand
choices.why: Speaking on what you do not know well spends the reputation the other talks built.

choices.text: Ignore the invitation
choices.why: Silence is not a no.

choices.text: Decline, and suggest a colleague who knows it
choices.why: Right: a no with an alternative, and sponsorship given outside.

choices.text: Accept, and talk about her own database instead
choices.why: Answering a different question, which lesson 5 warns against.
